title: The Dragons Came Back Hungry. 'House of the Dragon' Season 3 Lands on JioHotstar — and It Opens With a Death.
excerpt: Eight episodes, weekly drops, and a 72-minute premiere that drowns one of Rhaenyra's sons in the Battle of the Gullet. Here's where the diaspora can watch the bloodiest Targaryen chapter yet.
body:
There is a moment in the Season 3 premiere of House of the Dragon when the sea itself turns against a Targaryen, and you realise this show has finally stopped negotiating. After two years away — two years of fan theories, casting leaks, and the kind of waiting that only a *Game of Thrones* spin-off can demand — the dragons are back, and they are not back to talk.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=xZUavocHU2g

The season premiered Sunday, June 21, at 9 PM ET on HBO and Max in the United States, and dropped for Indian and diaspora viewers on JioHotstar the following day. And it announces itself immediately. The opening episode runs a luxurious 72 minutes, the longest the series has attempted, and it spends that runtime on the Battle of the Gullet — the open-water bloodbath fans of George R.R. Martin's *Fire & Blood* have been bracing for since the show began.

https://x.com/Uc_heyy02/status/2069300095737123297

> "Showrunner Ryan Condal, now steering the ship alone, has promised a season that trades the chess-board plotting of earlier years for open war, and the premiere keeps the promise with interest."

What the battle takes is not cheap. By the end of the maritime carnage, both the Triarchy and the Velaryon fleet lie shattered, Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint) is lost beneath the waves, and — in the image that has the internet reeling — Jacaerys "Jace" Velaryon (Harry Collett) is picked off like a fish in a barrel after his dragon is dragged under. Rhaenyra's eldest son. Her heir. Gone in the first hour.

> The slow-burn show that built two seasons on whispered conspiracies just opened its third with a body count.

That tonal shift is the whole point. Showrunner Ryan Condal, now steering the ship alone, has promised a season that trades the chess-board plotting of earlier years for open war, and the premiere keeps the promise with interest. The Dance of the Dragons — the Targaryen civil war that fractures a dynasty — is no longer looming. It's here, and it's airborne.

The ensemble returns in formidable shape. Matt Smith is back as Daemon Targaryen, all coiled menace, and Emma D'Arcy brings a colder, more haunted Rhaenyra to a war she can no longer pretend to control. On the green side, Olivia Cooke's Alicent Hightower curdles further into regret, Tom Glynn-Carney's Aegon II nurses his wounds and his grudges, and Ewan Mitchell's Aemond — the season's most magnetic villain — looks ready to set the realm alight. They are joined by a deep bench of newcomers including James Norton as Ormund Hightower and Dan Fogler as Torrhen Manderly.

For the diaspora, the practical news is the good news. All eight episodes roll out weekly on JioHotstar, mirroring the HBO Sunday-night cadence, with the finale landing August 9 in the US (and the early hours of August 10 elsewhere). Episode 2 arrives June 28. There is no binge here — this is appointment television, the kind that has NRI group chats from New Jersey to Wembley syncing their Sunday nights and dodging spoilers across time zones until they can catch up.

What to know before you press play

If you fell off somewhere in Season 2, the premiere does you the courtesy of a brutal recap-by-action: the politics are over, the dragons are weapons, and loyalty is a luxury nobody can afford. The season runs eight episodes, one step down from Season 1's ten and level with Season 2 — lean by design, every hour built to escalate.

There is also a clock ticking on the whole saga. HBO confirmed back in late 2025 that a fourth season will be the show's last, which reframes everything about Season 3: this is the penultimate movement, the stretch where the war stops gathering and starts ending. Expect the deaths to keep coming, and expect them to hurt.

The Targaryens always insisted that fire and blood was a family motto. Three seasons in, *House of the Dragon* has finally taken them at their word.
